newsitem.title: USA: Congress mulls bigger payoff from US ag research.
newsitem.headline: Congress mulls bigger payoff from US ag research.

text.p: Congress would ask a bigger payoff from agricultural research and discourage "earmarking" of funds for local projects under a discussion paper circulated by the Senate Agriculture Committee.

The government spends about $1.8 billion a year on ag research and extension services. There have been complaints the money is not fairly distributed among institutions and that some is squandered on picayune work of little value.
When Congress passed the "Freedom to Farm" law in 1996, it set a deadline of this fall to reauthorize ag research programs as a way to allow a thorough review.

Several changes were proposed in the Senate discussion paper to put a tighter focus on ag research. Committee chairman Richard Lugar, Indiana Republican, has said he wants to revamp the research sector.
Closed-door sessions involving senators and staff workers were expected throughout June to assemble, as much as possible, a bill. Funding level for research in the future was an open issue.
Hearings on ag research were to begin in mid-June before the House Agriculture Committee. Staff work to draft a bill could begin in July.

Lawmakers were enthused about the idea of setting research priorities through advisory committees whose membership would include farmers and business representatives, said a House Agriculture Committee worker who asked not to be named.
"Commodity groups are not reaching any accord among themselves" on dramatic change, the staff worker said, nor were lawmakers showing zeal for a top-to-bottom restructuring.
In light of the relatively slow start to legislation, there already is talk of extending the deadline to pass a bill.

There is some demand for change, however. The National Academy of Sciences recently suggested more regional research and collaboration instead of an uncoordinated doling out of money to the big-name universities.

Under the Senate discussion paper, funding to land grant universities and the Extension Service would be targeted to priority projects selected by advisory committees. Work "must be of multistate or national relevance," it said, freezing out local-interest projects.
Matching funds, not donation of in-kind services, would be required for special grants.
Any college, including historically black and tribal colleges, could seek the competitive grants awarded by the Extension Service -- a larger field of competitors than now.
Also under the draft, the $100 million a year Fund for Rural America would be dedicated to ag research.

Earlier this week, the Agriculture Department announced it had arranged an Academy of Sciences review of ag research programs to see if they were biased in favor of large farms. Acting Undersecretary Catherine Woteki said the review should not impinge on congressional reauthorization work.
